opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about it as a few different axes that all have to move together. If you push on only one, you hit a wall pretty quickly.

The first is hardware. A lot of what's happened over the last decade or so comes from the fact that neural networks have a very particular computational profile: lots of dense linear algebra, and they're surprisingly tolerant of reduced precision. That's why we started building TPUs. Once you realize you don't need general-purpose CPUs for this, you can build much more specialized, efficient chips, and then connect thousands of them with high-bandwidth interconnects so they act like one giant machine.

The second is systems and software. Having the hardware isn't enough. You need the right abstractions so researchers can express a model once and have it partitioned across many chips, with model parallelism, data parallelism, and pipelining handled for them. A lot of the work on things like Pathways was about letting you run computations across very large sets of accelerators without each researcher hand-tuning everything.

The third is algorithmic and modeling improvements, and people sometimes underestimate how much they contribute. If you look at the gains over time, a big fraction comes from better architectures, like Transformers versus recurrent models, better training recipes, sparsity and mixture-of-experts so you only activate part of the model for a given input, distillation, and better data. Those algorithmic gains compound with hardware gains. You get maybe 10x from hardware, 10x from algorithms, and suddenly you're two orders of magnitude ahead.

And then there's data, the quality and mix of what you train on, which matters as much as raw quantity.

So my mental model is that these are multiplicative. The best progress comes when you co-design them: the ML researchers tell the hardware folks what computations matter, the hardware folks say "if you could make your model look like this, we could make it 10x faster," and you iterate. That's been one of the more productive loops we've had.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I tend to think about it as three or four different kinds of progress that all have to happen roughly together, and if any one of them lags, the whole thing kind of stalls.

The first is algorithmic progress. Fundamental advances like the Transformer, or the realization that you can train sparsely activated models where only a small part of the network is used for any given example, those give you big step changes in what you can do per unit of compute. And then there are a lot of smaller things, like better optimizers, better ways of doing attention, distillation, that compound over time.

The second is hardware. We've seen huge gains from building hardware that's specialized for the kinds of computation these models actually do, which is mostly dense linear algebra at reduced precision. When we started on TPUs, part of the insight was that you don't need 32-bit floating point for inference, and later for training, and if you're willing to give that up you can get an order of magnitude more operations per watt. And then connecting many of those chips together with really high-bandwidth interconnect so you can treat a whole pod as one big machine.

The third, which I think people underappreciate, is the software and systems layer that lets you actually use that hardware at scale. How do you partition a model across thousands of chips? How do you overlap communication with computation? How do you make the system robust to a chip failing in the middle of a multi-week training run? A lot of my career has really been about that layer, going back to MapReduce and Bigtable and then DistBelief and TensorFlow. If you have great algorithms and great hardware but your utilization is 20 percent, you've thrown away most of your gains.

And then the fourth is data. Scaling the model only helps if you have data that's rich enough and diverse enough to make use of that extra capacity, and increasingly that means multimodal data, not just text.

What's interesting is that these feed back on each other. Better hardware lets you try algorithmic ideas you couldn't afford before. Algorithmic ideas, like sparsity, change what you want the hardware to look like. So you really want people working across those boundaries rather than in separate silos, and that's been a lot of how we've tried to organize things.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few complementary kinds of progress. One is computational: how do you build hardware and distributed systems that let you train larger models efficiently? Having lots of accelerators is useful only if you can keep them busy, move data where it needs to go, and avoid spending all your time communicating between them.

Another is algorithmic. Can you get the same quality with less computation, or better quality with the same computation? Improvements in model architectures, optimization, and numerical methods can be just as valuable as building a faster computer.

And then there’s the data and the training objective. What are you asking the model to learn, and are you giving it the right examples to learn that? Scaling a poor objective very efficiently doesn’t necessarily get you the capabilities you want.

These things interact. An algorithm might look attractive mathematically but be difficult to run efficiently on the hardware you have. So I think a lot of the opportunity comes from considering the whole system together. When those improvements reinforce one another, you can make substantially more progress than you would by focusing on any one dimension.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to think about it as a combination of progress in algorithms, hardware, and the systems that connect those two. You can have a much faster accelerator, but if you can’t feed it data or communicate efficiently between accelerators, you won’t get the benefit of that hardware.

On the algorithmic side, the question is: how much computation do we need to get a particular level of quality? Better architectures, optimization methods, and ways of using data can all move that curve. Then there’s the systems work of making those ideas run efficiently across a large collection of machines.

And those things interact. An algorithm that looks attractive in terms of arithmetic operations might have communication patterns that make it difficult to scale. So I think the biggest opportunities often come from looking across those boundaries—designing the model, the software, and the hardware together, rather than optimizing each independently.
